summary: This informational memo describes version 1.5 of RWhois, a client and server protocol for a distributed system to discover, retrieve and maintain directory information.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book that points you to other phone books until you find the right entry.

questions: what is the difference between whois and rwhois
subtitle: A directory protocol that hands you from server to server, following the hierarchy of a domain name or IP network, until you reach the one that holds the data.

tldr.problem: The original centralized Whois database could not keep up with a global Internet, and keeping it all in one place was too much effort.
tldr.mechanism: RWhois splits data across servers by authority area, named by a hierarchical label such as a domain name or CIDR network. A server that cannot answer returns a referral to a server closer to the data, and the client repeats its query there.
tldr.outcome: Version 1.5 adds multiple authority areas per server, data replication, a revised schema model, revised routing rules and revised error codes. The memo is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1714.

today: RFC 2167 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1714. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo itself says it specifies no Internet standard.

sections.title: From One Whois to Many
sections.content:
Early in the ARPANET, the SRI-NIC kept a centralized Whois database of hosts, networks and the email addresses of users (RFC 954). The RFC says the sheer size and effort of maintaining a centralized database called for a decentralized approach.

RWhois (Referral Whois) extends the Whois idea in a hierarchical, scaleable way. It distributes network objects, data representing Internet resources or people, and uses the hierarchical nature of domain names, IP networks and email addresses to find them. The structure borrows from the Domain Name System (RFC 1034), directory ideas from X.500 and influences from SMTP (RFC 821).

The specification covers both a directory access protocol (the syntax of the client and server interaction) and a directory architecture (the concepts the protocol implements). It uses SHOULD and SHALL as defined in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: One giant phone book got too big to keep up to date. RWhois lets many smaller phone books share the job.

sections.title: Schema, Objects and Authority Areas
sections.content:
Data is split across servers using a lexically hierarchical label: a text string whose place in a hierarchy can be worked out from the string itself. Phone numbers are one example; domain names such as war.west.netsol.com and CIDR networks such as 198.41.0.0/22 are the Internet ones. A person's name is not lexically hierarchical.

An authority area is a piece of the distributed database tied to a server and a hierarchical label, which is its name. It speaks with authority for its part of the hierarchy: it either returns the object, returns a referral to a sub-authority area, or says no objects were found. Each authority area is autonomous and treated as a separate database by the protocol. Linked areas form an RWhois tree with a root authority area.

There is no standard database schema, but every class must include the base class attributes: Class-Name, Auth-Area, ID, Updated, Guardian, Private and TTL. Two standard classes should be in every implementation: the referral class (Referred-Auth-Area, Referral) and the guardian class (Guard-Scheme, Guard-Info). Attributes have a type: TEXT, ID or SEE-ALSO.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone book is in charge of one neighborhood of names. It either has your entry, points to a smaller book, or says there is none.

sections.title: Referrals and Query Routing
sections.content:
A referral is the location of another server, holding its host name (or IP address), port number and authority area. The server can forward the query itself or return the referral to the client. A link referral points down the tree to a more specific server; a punt referral points up toward the root.

For each query term the server follows the routing rules. If the search value is hierarchical and inside one of its authority areas, it returns a link referral when a referral object covers it, or the 230 No objects found error when none does. If the value is hierarchical but outside all its areas, it returns a punt referral. If every term is non-hierarchical, it may ask a special index server for referrals and pass them on.

Several referrals can come back at once; the client may follow them in any order. If all of them name the same authority area, the client should follow only one. To follow a referral the client connects to the given host and port and issues the same query.
sections.plainLanguage: If a librarian cannot find your book, she points you to the right shelf, or up to the head librarian. You keep following the pointers until you get the book.

sections.title: The Client and Server Conversation
sections.content:
A session goes: the client connects, the server sends a banner with its protocol versions and capabilities, the client may send directives, then a query, and the server returns results and closes the connection unless told otherwise. By default the server closes after each query; the -holdconnect directive changes that.

A directive is a command whose first character is a hyphen, used to set session controls or fetch meta-information. Only -rwhois is required; the others (-class, -directive, -display, -forward, -holdconnect, -limit, -notify, -quit, -register, -schema, -security, -soa, -status, -xfer) are optional. Every response line starts with % and the last line is %ok or %error <code> <text>.

A query must not begin with a hyphen. The server must support unrestricted, class-restricted and attribute-restricted queries (attribute=search-string), and may support boolean and/or and a wild card asterisk. Results use the dump format, <class-name>:<attribute-name>;<type character>:<attribute-value>, with type characters T, I and S. The protocol runs over TCP by default and may use UDP for a single quick query; either way servers should use port 4321 if available.
sections.plainLanguage: You say hello, the server says who it is, you ask your question, and it answers. Lines starting with a percent sign are the server talking about how things went.

sections.title: Replication Between Servers
sections.content:
Data is copied per authority area. A master (primary) server is where data is registered, and there must be exactly one for an area. Slave (secondary) servers copy the data, answer authoritatively and must not register data. The RFC recommends putting master and slave servers in different geographic places so one network outage does not stop the service.

A slave can copy whole classes or just some attributes, either all of the data (complete replication) or only what changed (incremental replication). Timing is controlled by start of authority (SOA) variables set at the master: Serial-Number, Refresh-Interval, Increment-Interval, Retry-Interval, Time-To-Live, Admin-Contact, Tech-Contact, Hostmaster and Primary-Server. A master may also send the -notify update directive so slaves update immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: One book is the original, and a few copies sit in other places. The copies check back with the original from time to time, so nobody is stuck if one place is closed.

sections.title: Guardians and Access Control
sections.content:
Security is built on the guardian class. Any data or meta-information in an authority area can point to one or more guardian objects; satisfying any one of them is enough, and a guardian with no guardian of its own guards itself. Two standard methods exist: password, which gives authentication only, and PGP, which gives authentication and encryption. PGP is the recommended method.

For updates, guardians linked to an area's SOA and schema information control who may add objects or change that information, and modification or deletion of single objects can be delegated per object. For access, a slave must satisfy a master's guardian to transfer data, and the master may encrypt it. Whole classes or single attributes can be made private by setting the Private property.
sections.plainLanguage: Some pages in the phone book have a lock. You need the right key, like a password, before you can change or read them.

viz.caption: LINK AND PUNT REFERRALS (EXAMPLE FROM RFC 2167)

messages.label: %rwhois V-1.5:00ffff:00 master.rwhois.net
messages.note: Banner sent when the connection opens.

messages.label: -holdconnect on
messages.note: Keep the connection open between queries.

messages.label: %referral rwhois://master.b.rwhois.net:4321/auth-area=b.rwhois.net
messages.note: A link referral down the tree.

messages.label: %referral rwhois://rs.internic.net:4321/auth-area=.
messages.note: A punt referral to the root authority area.
